A regular hexagon with side length 4 is subdivided into a lattice of 96 equilateral triangles of side length 1. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of this lattice. Compute the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in $S$ that contain the center of the hexagon strictly in their interior.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(O\) be the center of the hexagon. We will count the lattice vertices by the rays from \(O\).

Use the triangular-lattice basis
\[
u=(1,0),\qquad v=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),
\]
so a lattice vertex is \(iu+jv\) with integers \(i,j\). With this orientation the hexagon of side length \(4\) is
\[
|i|\le 4,\qquad |j|\le 4,\qquad |i+j|\le 4.
\]

Group the nonzero lattice vertices by the ray from \(O\) to them. In the \(60^\circ\) sector between \(u\) and \(v\), the points have \(i,j\ge 0\) and \(i+j\le 4\). Grouping them by ray gives the following rays in increasing angle:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{primitive ray direction} & \text{number of lattice points on that ray}\\
\hline
(1,0) & 4\\
(3,1) & 1\\
(2,1) & 1\\
(1,1) & 2\\
(1,2) & 1\\
(1,3) & 1
\end{array}
\]

Thus, around the full hexagon, the ray weights repeat as
\[
(4,1,1,2,1,1)
\]
six times. There are \(36\) rays and \(60\) nonzero lattice vertices.

For three chosen distinct rays, the center is strictly inside the triangle formed by choosing one lattice point on each ray exactly when the three angular gaps between the rays are all less than \(180^\circ\). Equivalently, the three rays are not contained in any closed half-plane through \(O\).

Let the ray weights be \(w_i\). The total number of weighted triples of distinct rays is
\[
\sum_{i<j<k} w_iw_jw_k.
\]
One period \((4,1,1,2,1,1)\) has
\[
\sum w=10,\qquad \sum w^2=24,\qquad \sum w^3=76.
\]
Over six periods,
\[
W=60,\qquad W_2=144,\qquad W_3=456.
\]
Hence the total weighted ray-triple count is
\[
T=\frac{W^3-3WW_2+2W_3}{6}
=\frac{60^3-3\cdot60\cdot144+2\cdot456}{6}
=31832.
\]

Now subtract the weighted ray triples that fail to contain \(O\) in the interior.

### 1. Triples lying in an open semicircle
For each ray as the smallest-angle ray, the other two rays must lie among the next \(17\) rays; the \(18\)-th ray is antipodal. The \(18\) consecutive rays starting at a ray have total weight \(30\) and square-sum \(72\). If the starting ray has weight \(a\), the next \(17\) rays have total weight \(30-a\) and square-sum \(72-a^2\), so their unordered pair-product sum is
\[
\frac{(30-a)^2-(72-a^2)}{2}.
\]
Among the \(36\) rays:
- \(a=1\) occurs \(24\) times: contribution \(\frac{29^2-71}{2}=385\);
- \(a=2\) occurs \(6\) times: contribution \(\frac{28^2-68}{2}=358\);
- \(a=4\) occurs \(6\) times: contribution \(\frac{26^2-56}{2}=310\).

Thus the open-semicircle count is
\[
24\cdot385+6\cdot358+6\cdot310=13248.
\]

### 2. Triples containing an antipodal pair of rays
An antipodal pair has common weight \(a\). The third ray can be any of the other rays, giving total weight \(60-2a\). So a pair contributes
\[
a^2(60-2a).
\]
There are \(3\) antipodal pairs of weight \(4\), \(3\) of weight \(2\), and \(12\) of weight \(1\). Hence this count is
\[
3\cdot4^2(60-8)+3\cdot2^2(60-4)+12\cdot1^2(60-2)
=3864.
\]

Therefore the number of valid weighted ray triples is
\[
31832-13248-3864=14720.
\]

Each such weighted ray triple corresponds to exactly one nondegenerate triangle whose interior strictly contains the center.

\[
\boxed{14720}
\]
